newsitem.title: CHINA: First official U.S. cherry shipment lands in China.
newsitem.headline: First official U.S. cherry shipment lands in China.

text.p: The first official shipment of Washington cherries to China since the 1995 signing of a bilateral agreement has arrived in Shanghai, but the high price is likely to keep them off Chinese shopping lists for now.
The cherries arrived in China's biggest city by courier flight late on Thursday in time for a Friday promotion organised by the U.S. Agricultural Trade Office, Shanghai director Scott Reynolds said.
At a C&F (cost and freight) price of $50-60 per 20-lb (9-kg) case, the cherries would retail in Shanghai at 70-80 yuan ($8.40-9.60) per lb, he said.

"This is the first year, so we don't expect to sell huge amounts in the Chinese market straight away," he said, adding that some Chinese importers had expressed interest but no commercial orders had yet been made.
The cherries would cost about $1.50-2.00 a lb in the United States but were subject to a 48-percent import tariff in China and a value-added tax, U.S. officials said.

The signing of the protocol in 1995 under which China agreed to import Washington cherries was considered a breakthrough at the time and came after exhaustive phytosanitary, or food safety, talks focusing on plant safety issues.
It was the result of a March 1995 pact between Beijing and Washington in which China agreed to protect U.S. copyrights and base its food safety standards of plant and animal imports on sound science.
In return, Washington agreed to support China's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
U.S. officials said on Friday they hoped the tariffs now applicable to the cherries would be dealt with as part of China's WTO membership application.
They said that while this is the first official shipment, Washington cherries had already entered China, most probably through the porous southern ports, via Hong Kong.
This has also been true of other U.S. fruits and foodstuffs, the sources said.
This year's harvest of Northwest U.S. sweet cherries was expected to be 48,700 tonnes of Bing, Lambert and Rainier variety cherries, Reynolds said.
The season lasts just six weeks, with prices coming down during the season. But as a highly perishable product, the cherries had to be air-freighted to overseas markets, he said.
